content: 1. None of the included studies reported occurrences of maternal death, allergic reactions, or irritation at the surgical site. Similarly, neonatal infections and severe neonatal morbidity were not documented in any of the studies. 2. The trials included in the analysis utilized various combinations of antiseptic agents and application methods. For example, some trials compared scrubbing versus painting techniques using the same antiseptic agent. 3. When comparing chlorhexidine gluconate (CHX) to povidone-iodine (PVP-I), the trials demonstrated variability in the methods of application both within and between studies. This variability may have introduced confounding factors that affected the accuracy of the effect estimates. It is important to note that manufacturers recommend different application methods for CHX and PVP-I. 4. The Cochrane review also included a comparison of the use of incise drapes versus non-incise drapes in three trials. One of these trials was included in the antiseptic agent comparison section, as it evaluated isopropyl alcohol scrub plus iodophor-impregnated drape versus iodophor scrub alone, alongside the use of incise drapes. The other two trials compared the use of antiseptic agents with or without incise drapes but used the same antiseptic agents in both arms, and thus were excluded from this framework. 5. Three trials investigating the effect of application techniques with comparable antiseptic compounds found no significant differences in surgical site infection rates. 6. Despite the known antimicrobial activity of many antiseptic agents, the optimal approach to surgical site preparation remains unclear. The WHO panel strongly recommends alcohol-based antiseptic solutions containing CHX for preoperative skin preparation in patients undergoing surgical procedures, based on low to moderate quality evidence. 7. A systematic review of qualitative studies on women’s perspectives and experiences with antibiotics and antiseptics for infection prevention during childbirth identified one study involving 21 women in the United Kingdom. These women described their recovery after cesarean section, focusing on pain, mobility limitations, caregiving challenges, and concerns about wound infection or non-healing. Many women reported receiving inadequate information about the risks of postoperative infections, including endometritis. 8. A 2018 core outcome set for maternal infectious morbidity following cesarean delivery was proposed based on a systematic review of 452 trials and a Delphi survey of 40 review authors. The proposed outcomes included endometritis (primary outcome), maternal mortality, wound infection, wound complications, febrile morbidity, and neonatal morbidity. 9. A systematic review of qualitative studies on women’s preferences for intrapartum care found that most women desire a positive birth experience with good outcomes for both mother and baby. However, they acknowledge that medical interventions may sometimes be necessary. Women, particularly first-time mothers, often feel apprehensive about labor and birth and are cautious about medical interventions, though they may welcome them in certain contexts to address recognized complications. 10. The Cochrane systematic review comparing CHX to PVP-I for preoperative skin antiseptics across various types of surgeries (e.g., foot/ankle, plastic, shoulder, vaginal, laparotomy, mastectomy, and cesarean section) found no included studies that specifically focused on cesarean sections. 11. A cost analysis conducted at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania determined that switching from PVP-I to CHX resulted in net cost savings of $16–$26 per surgical case. Sensitivity analyses confirmed that these savings persisted under most circumstances. 12. The availability of supplies required for infection control procedures, such as antiseptic solutions, gloves, and running water, varies across lowand middle-income countries. The quality of antiseptic solutions may also differ between settings. Overall, the use of antiseptics is likely to increase health equity by preventing deaths and serious health consequences of peripartum infections with an inexpensive and easily implemented intervention. 13. WHO guidelines on surgical site infections note that the use of alcohol-based antiseptic agents may be refused by patients or healthcare workers for religious reasons. Engaging cultural and religious leaders has proven useful in overcoming such barriers, as demonstrated by the Muslim Scholars’ Board’s statement allowing the use of alcohol-containing medicines when necessary. 14. A systematic review on the perspectives of women and healthcare providers regarding antiseptic use at birth identified that non-compliance with antiseptic guidelines among healthcare providers is influenced by factors such as lack of supervision and training, inadequate supply, absence of relevant policies, doubts about benefits, perceived lack of clinical evidence, and insufficient examples or directives from senior colleagues. 15. The WHO panel considered the intervention of preoperative skin preparation with antiseptic agents to be feasible, as it is a routine practice performed by skilled health personnel during cesarean sections.
